UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT
Pre-Training

Jungwoo Park Affiliation: Korea University Affiliation: AIGEN Sciences    Taewhoo Lee & Jaewoo Kang ††thanks: Work done prior to joining Amazon.††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Korea University Affiliation: AIGEN Sciences Affiliation: Amazon {jungwoo-park,taewhoo,kangj}@korea.ac.kr Model:UltraBERT-150M UltraBERT-380M
Abstract

Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.

1 Introduction

Bidirectional encoders remain essential for non-generative applications, even amid the rapid progress of decoder-only large language models (LLMs). Their modest inference cost allows them to embed or score large volumes of text efficiently, making them the backbone of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines (Lewis et al., 2020), quality filtering of pre-training data (Penedo et al., 2024), and reward modeling for reinforcement learning (Gisserot-Boukhlef et al., 2026b). While decoders owe much of their popularity to their generalization to unseen tasks, fine-tuned encoders have often been shown to match much larger decoders on well-defined tasks at a fraction of the cost (Bucher and Martini, 2024; Edwards and Camacho-Collados, 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b).

Recent work has increasingly modernized encoders with innovations from decoder-only LLMs (Portes et al., 2023; Warner et al., 2025; Breton et al., 2025), adopting architectural advances such as rotary position embeddings (Su et al., 2024), FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024), along with token scaling (Sardana et al., 2024). However, the pre-training recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions. In particular, the masked language modeling (MLM) objective, which is specific to encoders, is still configured with lessons from prior studies under limited token budgets (Wettig et al., 2023; Gisserot-Boukhlef et al., 2026a), where convergence speed is entangled with final performance. This core component trades off classification against retrieval, leaving encoders trained with a single configuration specialized, with no single model performing competitively on both.

In this work, we begin by revisiting encoder pretraining at scale, and reveal three key findings. (1) Training encoders on up to 8.8T tokens, we find that downstream performance saturates around 1–2T tokens even as training and validation losses keep decreasing, unlike decoders, which continue to improve. This indicates an upper bound that additional tokens cannot raise. (2) At saturation, where convergence speed no longer confounds the comparison, classification consistently favors lower masking ratios across model sizes, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models, whereas retrieval favors higher ones. (3) Unlike in decoders, pruning and distillation from a stronger teacher does not uniformly raise encoder performance: it improves classification at a low masking ratio but degrades retrieval at a high one.

Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, which reconciles the two masking regimes within a single encoder rather than settling for a single configuration. Observing that the two regimes shape the LM head into distinct geometries, we propose LM head decoupling, which mixes 5% and 50% masked sequences within each batch while assigning a separate LM head to each ratio. Furthermore, we restrict distillation to the low-ratio sequences, while training the high-ratio ones with standard MLM. Starting from a 1.3B teacher, we obtain 380M and 150M models through pruning and distillation, trained on 2T tokens with native 32K context. Across classification and retrieval, where the strongest baseline differs, UltraBERT achieves state of the art on both, reaching 91.0 on GLUE (Wang et al., 2018) and 47.7 on BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021). Our 150M model matches RoBERTa-large (Liu et al., 2019) on classification with 2.3×\times fewer parameters, and outperforms Ettin-encoder-400M (Weller et al., 2026) on retrieval at 2.6×\times smaller size. Together, these results redefine what a single encoder can achieve, pushing encoder pretraining beyond its presumed limits.

2 Related Work

Modernized encoders

Since BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), the development of encoders has been slower than that of decoder-only LLMs. Recent work has revived encoders by bringing in innovations from LLMs, such as RoPE, GLU, and alternating local and global attention, along with trillions of training tokens (Portes et al., 2023; Nussbaum et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Warner et al., 2025; Breton et al., 2025; Weller et al., 2026). However, the pre-training recipe itself, in particular the MLM objective and its masking ratio, has been inherited from the conventions of the BERT era. As a result, each of these encoders excels on one side only, with none performing competitively across both classification and retrieval.

Masking ratio and pre-training objectives

The masking ratio of MLM has been revisited in several studies, which report that ratios higher than the original 15% are beneficial, especially for larger models (Wettig et al., 2023; Ankner et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Dong et al., 2025; Gisserot-Boukhlef et al., 2026a). However, these findings are based on budgets of 10B–100B tokens, where the effect of the masking ratio is entangled with convergence speed. Another line of work replaces MLM with Replaced Token Detection (RTD) (Clark et al., 2020; He et al., 2023), which is considered superior on classification tasks but is known to degrade retrieval (Rep et al., 2024; Warner et al., 2025). This comparison, however, has always been made at the conventional 15% masking, without varying the corruption level. In contrast, our work revisits both questions after reaching saturation with trillions of tokens, on both classification and retrieval tasks.

Encoders for retrieval

Bidirectional encoders are also widely adopted for information retrieval. Bi-encoders are trained to encode a given text into a single vector, which is aligned to be close to those of similar texts (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). They usually start from MLM pre-training to acquire basic linguistic knowledge, and then go through contrastive fine-tuning (Wang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Nussbaum et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). While the fine-tuning stage has been extensively optimized, the pre-training recipe of the backbone determines the upper bound of the resulting model. Encoders designed for retrieval, however, tend to fall behind on classification.

Knowledge distillation for language models

Knowledge distillation for encoders has been proposed to match various targets: masked token reconstruction logits (Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020), hidden state vectors (Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020), self-attention scores (Jiao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020), and Gram matrices of attention vectors (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021). Meanwhile, recent LLMs usually adopt logit-based distillation to develop small language models (Gemma Team et al., 2024; Gemma Team et al., 2025; Amini et al., 2025; Meta AI, 2024). In particular, Muralidharan et al. (2024) and Liu et al. (2026) propose Cascade Distillation, where a small model is initialized from the pruned weights of its parent and then distilled from a stronger teacher. However, whether these approaches transfer to encoders, and how they interact with the masking ratio, remains unexplored.

3 Exploring the Pre-Training Recipe for Stronger Encoders

In this section, we examine the core design choices of MLM pre-training under controlled settings. We train encoders at three scales (150M, 380M, and 1.3B) with RoPE and alternating local and global attention, similar to Warner et al. (2025). All experiments use the same dataset mixture and tokenizer. Following the evaluation protocol of Warner et al. (2025), we fine-tune and evaluate on GLUE (Wang et al., 2018) and SQuAD 2.0 (Rajpurkar et al., 2018) for classification, and fine-tune on MS MARCO (Nguyen et al., 2016) and report the average nDCG@10 on BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) for retrieval. Further details of the experimental setup are provided in Appendix A and B.

3.1 Training Token Scaling and Downstream Saturation

Prior work has demonstrated that decoder models continue to improve at extreme token scale (Sardana et al., 2024), and that their downstream task performance is also predictable alongside loss (Gadre et al., 2025). This raises a natural question: can encoder models also benefit from more training tokens? To answer this question, we train encoders at two scales (150M and 1.3B) on 8.8 trillion tokens, with a masking ratio of 30%. We then evaluate intermediate checkpoints on GLUE, SQuAD 2.0, and BEIR to observe how downstream performance evolves.

The results are shown in Figure 2. Encoders trained with the MLM objective saturate around 1–2 trillion tokens, while both training and validation losses keep decreasing. In particular, the BEIR scores saturate even earlier, showing no significant improvement beyond the first evaluation point of 275B tokens. These observations indicate that (1) encoders do not continue to improve on downstream tasks with more training tokens, and (2) unlike decoders, their fine-tuned downstream performance is not directly correlated with loss.

We then ask whether this saturation reflects a fundamental difference between encoders and decoders. To this end, we evaluate the intermediate checkpoints of our 1.3B encoder and the SmolLM2 1.7B decoder (Ben Allal et al., 2025) on 6 benchmarks most widely used for decoders. Figure 3 shows clearly divergent trends. For base models, both the encoder and decoder improve in 5-shot accuracy, and the decoder in particular exhibits a rapid rise known as emergent abilities (Wei et al., 2022). However, after instruction tuning on the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) format, the encoder saturates as on the previous downstream tasks, while the decoder keeps improving.

These results suggest that encoder models have an upper bound on downstream performance that additional pre-training tokens cannot raise. If we have enough compute budget to exceed the saturation point, how can we raise this upper bound itself? This question strongly motivates us to revisit the encoder pre-training methodology.

3.2 Masking Ratios and Classification Tasks

The MLM objective differs from the causal LM objective in one respect: the masking ratio. Its impact has been investigated in various contexts (Dong et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2023; Wettig et al., 2023; Gisserot-Boukhlef et al., 2026a; Boizard et al., 2025), yet its effect has been entangled with convergence speed. In this section, we revisit it from the perspective of downstream classification tasks, but after reaching saturation, where this entanglement no longer applies.

In detail, we train encoders at three scales with masking ratios up to 50%. As lower ratios require more tokens to converge (Wettig et al., 2023; Ankner et al., 2024), we allocate tokens accordingly11 1 We use 1T tokens at 50% and 30%, 2T tokens at 15%, and 5T tokens at 6% and 3%. Empirically, saturation occurred around 1–2T tokens at 15% and 2–3T tokens at 6% and 3%, so these budgets are sufficient. based on the saturation points identified in Section 3.1 and evaluate on GLUE and SQuAD 2.0.

Figure 4 shows that classification performance consistently degrades as the masking ratio increases, across all model sizes. This is contrary to prior work (Wettig et al., 2023; Gisserot-Boukhlef et al., 2026a; Dong et al., 2025), which finds larger masking ratios optimal for larger models. We attribute this discrepancy to eliminating the effect of convergence speed by using trillions of tokens, whereas prior results were confined to 10B–100B budgets. Notably, Wettig et al. (2023) argued that higher ratios are preferable since the gain from faster convergence outweighs the cost of corruption, treating the benefit of less corruption only briefly. At saturation, however, we find the limitation from corruption to be far more pronounced.

Impact of contextual corruption

To understand the effect of corruption on encoders, we further compare MLM with RTD. Conventionally, ELECTRA-style models are considered to be superior on classification tasks (Clark et al., 2020; He et al., 2023), and they remain so even against recent modernized encoders trained with MLM (Antoun et al., 2025), though at a critical cost on retrieval (Rep et al., 2024; Warner et al., 2025).

The superiority of RTD is often explained by its higher training efficiency (Clark et al., 2020). Training to saturation factors out this efficiency, allowing us to isolate what makes RTD superior beyond faster convergence. One remaining difference lies in contextual corruption, i.e., how contextually plausible the corrupted tokens are. In RTD, a generator fills masked tokens with semantically relevant alternatives, which are more informative than the [MASK] token. We hypothesize that this difference mainly explains the superiority.

We train 150M discriminators, with generators of half the depth, following He et al. (2023). Since the actual replacement ratio changes during training as the generator improves, we adjust the generator’s masking ratio so that the average replacement ratio matches that of MLM. We report the average score of GLUE and SQuAD 2.0, excluding CoLA.22 2 We discuss CoLA as a confounder in Appendix C.1.

Figure 5 shows the improvement of RTD over MLM. As the corruption ratios of the two objectives are not exactly the same, Figure 5(b) is computed by interpolating both curves. The gap peaks around 15%, the masking ratio adopted by Clark et al. (2020) and He et al. (2023), and diminishes toward both ends for different reasons. Around 50%, the generator has too little context, resulting in trivial replacements, which are known to bring no gain over MLM (Di Liello et al., 2022). Around 3%, the difference between plausible alternatives and [MASK] tokens becomes negligible, as the absolute corruption level is small. In practice, since classification favors low masking ratios in the first place, encoders can retain MLM without sacrificing classification, avoiding the retrieval degradation that RTD entails.

3.3 Masking Ratios and Retrieval Tasks

Lower masking ratios favor classification, but it is unclear whether the same holds for downstream retrieval tasks, the other major application of bidirectional encoders. Beyond the classification tasks, we now examine retrieval, reporting the average nDCG@10 on BEIR as the downstream performance. Figure 6(a) shows the opposite trend to classification. The masking ratio of 50% consistently achieves the highest score across all model scales, which is also in line with a few prior works (Boizard et al., 2025; Gisserot-Boukhlef et al., 2026a). Overall, no single masking ratio is optimal for both classification and retrieval.

To understand why higher masking ratios benefit retrieval, we look into what changes in the representation space. We measure the effective rank (Roy and Vetterli, 2007) of the mean-pooled vectors of each trained model. The effective rank reflects how many dimensions in the representation space the model actually uses. As shown in Figure 6(b), the effective rank tends to increase with the masking ratio, indicating that higher masking ratios lead to higher utilization of the representation space.

We cannot tell whether the higher effective rank causes the improvement in retrieval, or whether the two are independent phenomena. Since using more dimensions is generally favorable for retrieval (Kusupati et al., 2022; Rottach et al., 2025), we ask whether the effective rank can be raised by regularization instead. As we need to use a lower masking ratio for classification, we train the encoder with 6% masking but try adopting the KoLeo regularizer (Sablayrolles et al., 2019), which is used for representation learning (Oquab et al., 2024; Siméoni et al., 2026). This encourages the vectors to spread isotropically, resulting in a higher effective rank (Zhang et al., 2025a).33 3 The relation between the KoLeo regularizer and the effective rank is explained in Appendix D.

Figure 6(c) and (d) compare the performances with and without the KoLeo regularizer on GLUE and BEIR, respectively. Raising the effective rank artificially cannot resolve the trade-off at hand: (1) the regularizer indeed improves BEIR but less than single 50% masking, and (2) it also harms the GLUE score. From this experiment, we confirm the strong contrast between classification and retrieval across masking ratios, and the limitation of using a single masking ratio.

3.4 Mixing Masking Ratios with LM Head Decoupling

From the previous sections, we observed that different masking ratios specialize encoders for different tasks, and that regularization cannot naturally resolve the trade-off. Since the two tasks favor opposite masking ratios, achieving the best of both without compromise can be viewed as multi-task learning (MTL). Under this view, we instead consider mixing multiple masking ratios within a batch, treating each ratio as a task and jointly optimizing their losses.

MTL frequently faces conflicts across tasks due to parameter sharing (Sener and Koltun, 2018; Yu et al., 2020). He et al. (2023) claimed that sharing input embeddings between the generator and discriminator leads to tug-of-war dynamics, where the two disturb each other, and resolved this with gradient-level disentanglement. Similarly, we observed the divergence of the encoders’ representation spaces through their effective rank in Section 3.3. We thus visualize the input embeddings and LM heads to look for such a conflict.

Figure 7 shows the geometry of both matrices for encoders trained with 6% and 50% masking. As illustrated, the LM heads take clearly different shapes, while the input embeddings are almost identical. The discrepancy is also observed in Figure 8, which plots the singular value spectra of the embeddings and LM heads. The LM head for 6% masking shows more concentrated singular values, indicating that the matrix occupies a lower-dimensional subspace. This is consistent with the model’s lower effective rank. The encoder’s gradients are computed from the loss through its LM head, so we conjecture that sharing it may cause gradient-level interference, and test decoupling the two heads.

We train encoders with various masking ratio mixing strategies, which have been explored in preliminary forms with different motivations: (1) decaying the ratio from 50% to 6% and 15% (Ankner et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023), and (2) sampling the ratio uniformly from 5% to 50% (Dong et al., 2025), denoted as 𝒰⁡(5%,50%)\mathcal{U}(5\%,50\%). Since performance on each task monotonically favors the opposite extreme, we further consider (3) combining 5% and 50% masked sequences within a batch, denoted as {5%,50%}\{5\%,50\%\}, with and without LM head decoupling. Note that 5% masking yields sparser gradient signals and converges more slowly than 50%, so we include four times more sequences masked at 5% in the batch.44 4 Contrary to common expectation, we found the convergence speed not proportional to the masking ratio, though lower ratios still converge slower. We evaluate all models on GLUE and BEIR.

Table 1 shows the results. Masking ratio decay brings no improvement over the single masking ratio on GLUE, and even harms it at 6% (88.8 vs 89.5). BEIR improves slightly, as the encoder is exposed to the larger ratio, yet still far from 45.0 of 50%. Either the early high corruption limits the upper bound, or the low-ratio phase needs to be much longer, which defeats the purpose of decay. Meanwhile, 𝒰⁡(5%,50%)\mathcal{U}(5\%,50\%), whose average ratio is 27.5%, performs almost the same as the single 30% (88.0 vs 88.3 on GLUE, both 44.2 on BEIR). Figure 9(a) and (b) also show that its LM head geometry is close to that of 30%. Mixing ratios over a range thus converges to the effect of the average.

In contrast, {5%,50%}\{5\%,50\%\} with decoupled LM heads achieves 89.4 on GLUE and 45.1 on BEIR, reaching the best scores of 6% (89.5) and 50% (45.0). Without decoupling, GLUE stays at 88.9, on par with the single 15%, while BEIR still improves from 43.8 to 44.7. Although exposure to the large masking ratio alone helps retrieval, these results suggest that sharing the LM head creates a conflict between masking regimes, which head decoupling alleviates. Figure 9(c) and (d) are consistent with this, where the decoupled heads for 5% and 50% take distinct geometries.

3.5 Revisiting Pruning and Distillation

We resolve the trade-off between classification and retrieval with LM head decoupling, but each is still bounded by what the model can reach on its own. To go beyond the limit, we revisit pruning and distillation, as in Sanh et al. (2019), Muralidharan et al. (2024), and Liu et al. (2026), under different masking ratios.

For distillation, we restrict ourselves to logit-based distillation, which is still widely used in recent LLMs. Attention-based distillation, including self-attention scores (Jiao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020) and Gram matrices (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021), requires O⁡(L2)O(L^{2}) memory and computational costs for length LL. These are unaffordable for long contexts and incompatible with FlashAttention.

All experiments are conducted at 15% and 50% masking. We first prune the trained 1.3B encoders to 380M following Muralidharan et al. (2024) and Liu et al. (2026), and distill each from its 1.3B parent on 500B tokens.55 5 As in prior work, distillation converges faster; we observe saturation at 250B tokens for 15% masking. We then evaluate on GLUE and BEIR, comparing with the 380M models trained from scratch. Results are presented in Table 2. For 15% masking, the distilled model indeed improves on GLUE (90.2 to 90.8), consistent with lower ratios benefiting classification, while BEIR remains the same. In contrast, the model distilled at 50% masking performs worse than the from-scratch model on BEIR (47.2 to 46.5). This is somewhat surprising, since we expected distillation to help the corresponding task. This degradation may come from the trivial signal of the teacher at 50% masking, similar to the interpretation of RTD in Section 3.2. Regardless of the underlying cause, pruning and distillation yield no gains over training from scratch at 50% masking, motivating us to apply distillation only at the low ratio.

4 UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT Pre-Training

Building on these findings, we introduce UltraBERT, a family of encoders in two sizes (150M and 380M) with 32K context that pushes the limit of existing encoders on both classification and retrieval without trade-off. Following Muralidharan et al. (2024) and Liu et al. (2026), we start from the 1.3B encoder as a teacher, prune it to 380M and then further to 150M, and distill both from the 1.3B teacher. Based on Section 3.4, we construct each batch with both 5% and 50% masking at a 4:1 ratio, with decoupled LM heads. Following Section 3.5, we apply KL divergence loss only to the 5% masked sequences, while the 50% ones are trained with the standard MLM loss. Figure 10 illustrates the framework, and the training setup follows Section 3 with the remaining details in Appendix A.

4.1 Evaluation Setup

To evaluate classification from various perspectives, we report GLUE and SQuAD 2.0 as in the ablation study. Furthermore, we include the English subset of MultiCoNER v2 (Fetahu et al., 2023) and Few-NERD (Ding et al., 2021) for the harder NER tasks. We also evaluate on RewardBench (Lambert et al., 2025) as a pairwise preference classification task. Each benchmark is fine-tuned with hyperparameter grid search on its training set (see Appendix B).

For the retrieval tasks, we follow Section 3 to report the BEIR score. Using the best model on BEIR, we report the code and math subsets of RAR-b (Xiao et al., 2024) to estimate generalizability in the code and math domains. To evaluate long context ability, we further fine-tune the best model on the English subset of MLDR (Chen et al., 2024) and report its test set score, alongside its LongEmbed (Zhu et al., 2024) score.

For all tasks, we compare with various model families as baselines: BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), MosaicBERT (Portes et al., 2023), NomicBERT (Nussbaum et al., 2025), GTE-en-MLM (Zhang et al., 2024), ModernBERT (Warner et al., 2025), Ettin Encoder (Weller et al., 2026), NeoBERT (Breton et al., 2025), and LFM2.5-Encoder (Liquid AI, 2026).

4.2 Results

As shown in Table 3, UltraBERT achieves state-of-the-art performance on almost all benchmarks. For the base size, UltraBERT achieves the best score on all benchmarks except MultiCoNER v2, where it still outperforms both ModernBERT and Ettin Encoder. For the medium size, UltraBERT achieves the best on all benchmarks except MLDR, where it is behind LFM2.5-Encoder-350M.

As the UltraBERT series natively supports 32K context length, both scales achieve the best score on LongEmbed, where even the base model outperforms the medium models of other families. Furthermore, the largest improvements are on code and math retrieval, with gains of 7.3 and 8.3 points at base and 8.4 and 7.7 points at medium over the second best, respectively.

Most importantly, previous encoders each excel in different areas. On GLUE, SQuAD 2.0, and RewardBench, Ettin Encoder was the best among prior models. On the NER tasks, NomicBERT, RoBERTa, and GTE-en-MLM led. On BEIR, ModernBERT was the strongest base model and LFM2.5-Encoder-350M the strongest medium model. None of them, however, reaches the top across the full range of benchmarks. UltraBERT is the first to do so at both scales, indicating that our recipe yields a truly general encoder rather than one specialized for a single task family.

5 Conclusion

We revisit the pre-training recipe of bidirectional encoders at the scale of trillions of tokens. Encoders saturate on downstream tasks at a few trillion tokens, beyond which the masking ratio determines their specialization: lower ratios favor classification, higher ratios favor retrieval. We reconcile the two by mixing both ratios within a batch with decoupled LM heads, and by applying logit-based distillation only at the low ratio. Built on these findings, UltraBERT achieves state-of-the-art results across classification and retrieval at both 150M and 380M with a 32K context, showing that the specialization of encoders is not inherent but a consequence of the recipe.

AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist in writing the proof in Appendix D, where the structure of the argument was designed by the authors and the AI assisted in formalizing the individual steps. We have not used generative AI tools to develop the conceptual framework, propose hypotheses, design experiments, implement methods, or interpret results; all training and evaluation code was written by the authors. The remaining tasks with required disclosure are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to edit the paper for readability, including converting result logs into LaTeX tables, to summarize and identify related literature, and to search for information. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: the proof in Appendix D was checked by the authors, all numbers in the tables were verified against the original logs, and all claims about prior work were checked against the original papers. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Ethics statement

This work pre-trains and evaluates general-purpose text encoders on publicly available datasets. The pre-training mixture consists of web, code, academic, and instruction data that are publicly released under their respective licenses, and we did not collect data from human subjects. As with any model trained on web-scale data, the encoders may inherit biases present in the training data, and downstream users should evaluate them for their use case. We do not foresee ethical concerns specific to this work beyond those common to encoder pre-training.

Reproducibility statement

We describe the architecture, optimization, pruning, and distillation in Appendix A, the pre-training data mixture with per-dataset token counts in Appendix A.3, and the fine-tuning and evaluation protocols for every benchmark, including hyperparameter grids and data sources, in Appendix B. The proof of the relation between the KoLeo regularizer and effective rank is given in Appendix D. Full per-task results are reported in Appendix E, along with the sources of baseline scores taken from the literature. We release the evaluation code, model weights and pre-training data mixture.

Appendix

Contents

Appendix A Training Setup

A.1 Architecture and Optimization

All encoders share the same architecture design. We use RoPE (Su et al., 2024), SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020), and alternating local and global attention similar to Warner et al. (2025), where every third layer applies global attention and the remaining layers apply local attention. The RoPE base is 10K for local attention and 640K for global attention, and the latter is increased to 2.56M during the 32K context extension. The LM head is untied from the input embeddings. We use the same tokenizer of SmolLM2 (Ben Allal et al., 2025), with a vocabulary of 49,152 tokens.66 6 https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/cosmo2-tokenizer

We scale the encoders by width while keeping the depth fixed at 24 layers. The hidden size grows from 768 for 150M to 1,024 for 380M and 2,048 for 1.3B, and the intermediate size of SwiGLU is set to 1,024, 3,072, and 5,632, respectively. The 150M model uses 6 attention heads and the two larger models use 8, with a head dimension of 128 for 150M and 380M and 256 for 1.3B.

We use AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, a weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The learning rate follows the warmup-stable-decay schedule (Hu et al., 2024), with 10B tokens of warmup and a decay phase over the last 10% of the token budget. Note that the learning rate is decayed to zero for every model evaluated in this paper, including the intermediate checkpoints in Section 3.1, each of which is obtained by branching a decay phase from the stable phase. We use a peak learning rate of 3e-4 for the experiments in Section 3, and 1e-4 for distillation and the final training of UltraBERT. The batch size is 4M tokens, with 2,048 sequences of 2,048 tokens. For UltraBERT, we train on 2T tokens in total, and extend the context length to 32K for the last 100B tokens (Gao et al., 2025).

Each model is trained on a single pod slice of TPU v4-512, v5e-256, or v6e-256, all with 256 chips. We use 16 data-parallel replicas with 16-way fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), and for the 32K context extension we reduce FSDP to 8-way and add 2-way tensor parallelism.

A.2 Pruning and Distillation

We derive the 380M and 150M encoders by reusing the best 1.3B encoder in Section 3.2 as the teacher, through Cascade Distillation (Liu et al., 2026), an iterative process of pruning and distillation: the 1.3B encoder is pruned to 380M and distilled, and the distilled 380M encoder is pruned again to 150M and distilled. We prune only along the width, keeping all 24 layers, following the observation of Muralidharan et al. (2024) that width pruning outperforms depth pruning at this scale. The 1.3B encoder is pruned to 380M by reducing the hidden size from 2,048 to 1,024, the head dimension from 256 to 128, and the intermediate size from 5,632 to 3,072, and the 380M encoder is pruned to 150M by reducing the hidden size to 768, the number of attention heads from 8 to 6, and the intermediate size to 1,024.

Following Muralidharan et al. (2024), we estimate the importance of hidden channels, attention heads, and FFN neurons from activations with forward passes only. As a calibration set, we take 2,000 documents from the pre-training mixture and pack them into 1,024 sequences of 1,024 tokens. For hidden channels, we use the output of the pre-attention normalization in each layer; for attention heads, the per-head output entering the output projection; and for FFN neurons, the gated activation entering the down projection. In all three cases, the activation magnitude is averaged over the sequence and then aggregated by the L2 norm over the batch. Hidden channel scores are further aggregated over layers, since the residual stream is shared across the network, whereas head and neuron scores are kept per layer. We keep the top-scoring channels, heads, and neurons.

When the head dimension is halved from 256 to 128, we reduce the query and key projections by keeping every other rotary frequency pair, so that the pairing of RoPE dimensions is preserved, and scale the query by 1/21/\sqrt{2} to keep the attention logits at the same magnitude. For the value and output projections, we apply a shared random orthogonal projection to the output of the value and the input of the output projection, which preserves their product in expectation.

Each pruned encoder is then distilled from the 1.3B teacher. As described in Section 3.5, we apply the KL divergence between the teacher and student logits on the 5% masked sequences, and the standard MLM loss on the 50% masked sequences. The 150M encoder is distilled from the same 1.3B teacher rather than from the 380M encoder, following Muralidharan et al. (2024) and Liu et al. (2026), who found that distilling from the original parent gives better results than distilling from the intermediate child.

A.3 Dataset Mixture

Table 4 lists the pre-training data mixture. Web data takes about two thirds of the budget, followed by code, academic papers, and mathematics. We also include a small portion of instruction data: FLAN and StackExchange, as in Weller et al. (2026), and Natural Reasoning. Although it is only 2.5% of the mixture, the encoder learns to follow instructions to some extent, which explains why the base model already works in the zero-shot and few-shot MCQA settings of Appendix B.3 and Figure 3. The model recognizes the MCQA format without any tuning, and the instruction data works well through the [MASK] position. This goes beyond the observation of Samuel (2024) that MLM-trained encoders can act as in-context learners: with instruction data in the mixture, the encoder follows instructions even in the zero-shot setting without demonstrations.

We also explored multi-stage training that adjusts the mixture ratios across stages, as in Ettin (Weller et al., 2026) and EuroBERT (Boizard et al., 2025). This is common practice for decoder LLMs (OLMo Team et al., 2024; Ben Allal et al., 2025), where upsampling high-quality data in the final stage has been shown to be effective. In our preliminary experiments with several mixture schedules, however, the downstream performance after fine-tuning was barely affected. We hypothesize that the exposure ratio of each dataset changes the token prediction distribution of the model, and thus its apparent zero-shot and few-shot performance, but has little effect on the intrinsic linguistic knowledge that fine-tuning builds on. We therefore use a single mixture throughout training.

Appendix B Evaluation Protocols

In this section, we detail the fine-tuning and evaluation protocols used throughout the paper. For the baselines in Table 3, we take scores from the literature where available, such as GLUE and SQuAD 2.0, and fine-tune and evaluate the rest ourselves under the same protocol.

B.1 Classification Tasks

For every fine-tuning run, we use AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}{=}0.9, β2=0.98\beta_{2}{=}0.98, ϵ=10−6\epsilon{=}10^{-6}, weight decay 0.1, gradient clipping at 1.0, a linear learning rate schedule with 5% warm-up, and bfloat16 mixed precision. Following the common practice of prior encoders (Liu et al., 2019; Warner et al., 2025; Weller et al., 2026), we perform a grid search per task and per model. The learning rate is always swept over {5​e-​6,8​e-​6,1​e-​5,3​e-​5,5​e-​5,8​e-​5}\{5\text{e-}6,8\text{e-}6,1\text{e-}5,3\text{e-}5,5\text{e-}5,8\text{e-}5\}, jointly with the task-specific maximum lengths, batch sizes, and epochs in Table 5. During each run, the model is evaluated on the development set periodically and the best checkpoint is kept. We then select the best configuration on the development set and report its score; for tasks with a labeled test set (MultiCoNER v2, Few-NERD), the test score of the selected configuration is reported.

GLUE

We evaluate on the 8 GLUE tasks (Wang et al., 2018) excluding WNLI, as in Devlin et al. (2019), and report development-set scores: Matthews correlation for CoLA, Pearson correlation for STS-B, accuracy on the matched set for MNLI, and accuracy for the remaining tasks. Inputs are truncated to 128 tokens. Following Liu et al. (2019), RTE, MRPC, and STS-B are initialized from the best MNLI checkpoint of the same model instead of the pre-trained weights. The large tasks (MNLI, QQP, QNLI, SST-2) use a batch size of 64 with {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\} epochs. The small tasks (CoLA, STS-B, MRPC, RTE) are known to be unstable (Portes et al., 2023; Nussbaum et al., 2025), so we sweep the batch size and {2,5,10}\{2,5,10\} epochs with 4 seeds, take the best development score over the grid for each seed, and report the median across the seeds.

SQuAD 2.0

We fine-tune on SQuAD 2.0 (Rajpurkar et al., 2018) with the same protocol as GLUE. Question–context pairs are truncated to 384 tokens with a document stride of 128. We sweep the batch size over {16,32,64}\{16,32,64\} and the number of epochs over {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}, and report the F1 score on the development set of the best configuration.

Named Entity Recognition

We adopt two fine-grained NER benchmarks, which are known to be more challenging and thus discriminative among models. MultiCoNER v2 (Fetahu et al., 2023) contains short, lower-cased sentences with 33 entity types; we use the English subset (16,778 / 871 / 249,980 sentences for training, development, and test). Since the development set is small, every configuration is run with 3 seeds, and the average development score is used for selection. Few-NERD (Ding et al., 2021) is used in its supervised setting with 66 entity types and the official split (131,767 / 18,824 / 37,648). To avoid tokenization mismatches with byte-level BPE tokenizers, we prepend a leading space to each word so that the pre-tokenized encoding is identical to that of the raw string. We compute entity-level F1 and report the test scores of the selected configurations: macro-F1 over entity types for MultiCoNER v2 and micro-F1 for Few-NERD.

RewardBench

To examine encoders as reward models, we fine-tune with the Bradley-Terry loss. The training pairs are the union of HuggingFaceH4/UltraFeedback-binarized (Cui et al., 2024) and Skywork/Skywork-Reward-Preference-80K-v0.2 (Liu et al., 2024), restricted to single-turn conversations. This yields 135,981 pairs, of which 5% (6,800 pairs) are held out as a development set. Prompts and responses are concatenated with a plain template (USER: and ASSISTANT:) and truncated to 1,024 tokens. Within each run, the epoch checkpoint with the lowest loss on the held-out pairs is kept. We compute the accuracy of the 4 sections (Chat, Chat Hard, Safety, and Reasoning) with the official per-subset weighting, and report their average.

B.2 Retrieval Tasks

For retrieval, we fine-tune each encoder as a single-vector dense retriever using mean pooling and the cached multiple negatives ranking loss (Gao et al., 2021). We use AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}{=}0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}{=}0.999, ϵ=10−8\epsilon{=}10^{-8} and no weight decay, together with gradient clipping at 1.0, a linear learning rate schedule with 5% warm-up, and bfloat16 mixed precision. Every model is trained with a per-device batch size of 512 on 8 GPUs, and evaluated with the mteb library (Muennighoff et al., 2023).

BEIR and RAR-b

Following the training setup of Warner et al. (2025) and Weller et al. (2026), we fine-tune on MS MARCO (Nguyen et al., 2016) with 1.25M hard-negative triplets from sentence-transformers/msmarco-co-condenser-margin-mse-sym-mnrl-mean-v1, using one epoch and a maximum length of 256 tokens. The learning rate is swept over {1​e-​5,3​e-​5,5​e-​5,8​e-​5,1​e-​4,2​e-​4,3​e-​4,5​e-​4,8​e-​4,1​e-​3}\{1\text{e-}5,\allowbreak 3\text{e-}5,\allowbreak 5\text{e-}5,\allowbreak 8\text{e-}5,\allowbreak 1\text{e-}4,\allowbreak 2\text{e-}4,\allowbreak 3\text{e-}4,\allowbreak 5\text{e-}4,\allowbreak 8\text{e-}4,\allowbreak 1\text{e-}3\}, and the checkpoint with the highest score on BEIR is selected to measure the best attainable retrieval performance of each backbone. We evaluate on the 15 BEIR datasets (Thakur et al., 2021), using the development split for MS MARCO and the mean over the 12 forums for CQADupstack, and report the average nDCG@10.

To estimate generalization to the code and math domains, the same checkpoint is evaluated on the code and math subsets of RAR-b (Xiao et al., 2024), which cast reasoning problems as retrieval. The code subset is curated from HumanEvalPack (Muennighoff et al., 2024), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), CodeSearchNet (Husain et al., 2019), and TinyCode77 7 https://huggingface.co/datasets/nampdn-ai/tiny-codes. The math subset is curated from MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and MetaMathQA (Yu et al., 2024). For each query, the ground-truth solution is retrieved from 301K and 389K candidates, respectively, and we report nDCG@10.

MLDR and LongEmbed

As MS MARCO passages are short, we further fine-tune the selected BEIR checkpoint on the English training triplets of MLDR (Chen et al., 2024), following the in-domain setting of Warner et al. (2025). We use 80K triplets from sentence-transformers/mldr and train with the same learning rate as the MS MARCO stage, with the maximum length set to the context length of each model, capped at 16K tokens. The resulting model is evaluated on the English test set of MLDR and on the 6 tasks of LongEmbed (Zhu et al., 2024), with the maximum length again set to the context length of each model, capped at 32K tokens. For LongEmbed, the 4 real tasks (NarrativeQA, QMSum, SummScreenFD, and 2WikiMultihopQA) are scored by nDCG@10, and the 2 synthetic tasks (Passkey and Needle) by recall@1 averaged over the 8 context lengths from 256 to 32K tokens. We report nDCG@10 on MLDR and the average over the 6 tasks on LongEmbed.

B.3 Zero-Shot and Few-Shot MCQA

To compare encoders and decoders on LLM-style benchmarks in Section 3.1, we evaluate 6 multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) benchmarks: ARC (Clark et al., 2018), BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), CommonsenseQA (Talmor et al., 2019), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), and SIQA (Sap et al., 2019). We use the test sets of ARC, MMLU, and OpenBookQA, and the validation sets of BoolQ, CommonsenseQA, and SIQA, whose test labels are not public. We report accuracy, averaged over the 57 subjects for MMLU and over the Easy and Challenge sets for ARC, and the final score is the average over the 6 benchmarks.

Prompting and Scoring

Each question is formatted with the prefix (Question:) followed by the options, and the suffix (Answer:). For BoolQ and SIQA, which come with contexts, the context is additionally prepended with the prefix Context:. For the few-shot setting, the first 5 examples of the development set of the same subject for MMLU, the validation set for ARC and OpenBookQA, and the training set for the others are prepended as demonstrations in the same format. Encoders and decoders share the prompt and differ only in how the answer is read out. For encoders, a single [MASK] token is appended after Answer: and the MLM logits at that position are compared over the option letters. For decoders, the next-token logits at the last position are used instead. For BoolQ, we compare the summed probabilities of the yes and no variants (Yes, yes, True, true vs. No, no, False, false). Inputs are truncated from the left to 2,048 tokens.

Instruction Tuning

Base models are evaluated in the 5-shot setting, and instruction-tuned models in the zero-shot setting. For instruction tuning, we use a subset of the FLAN collection (Longpre et al., 2023) with zero-shot templates that present answer options, sampling 100 to 1,000 examples from each of 718 tasks in Flan2021, P3, and NIv2, for a total of 545K examples. We keep the examples whose answers are at most 5 tokens long (480K), and hold out 1% for validation. Encoders are trained by appending as many [MASK] tokens as the answer length and predicting the answer tokens with the MLM head, and decoders with the standard causal LM loss on the answer tokens. Both are trained for 3 epochs with a batch size of 128, a learning rate of 5e-5, weight decay 0.01, a linear schedule with 10% warm-up, a maximum length of 256 tokens with left truncation, and bfloat16 mixed precision.

Appendix C Additional Analysis on Replaced Token Detection

C.1 CoLA as a Confounder

It has long been observed that RTD-trained encoders are particularly strong on CoLA. Di Liello et al. (2021) found that ELECTRA outperforms MLM and random-substitution variants by a wide margin only on CoLA, RTE, and STS-B, while the gap is not significant on the more stable tasks, and Xu et al. (2020) attributed the gain to the pre-training task of ELECTRA being more aligned with CoLA.

We observe the same in a controlled setting. Starting from the 150M encoder pre-trained with 50% masking in Section 3.2, we continue training with the RTD objective for only 100B tokens. As shown in Table 6, the average of the other GLUE tasks moves by 0.5 points, whereas CoLA jumps by 9.9 points, from 61.6 to 71.5. A short exposure to RTD is enough to change the CoLA score by an amount that no other task shows.

CoLA asks whether a sentence is linguistically acceptable, and RTD trains the encoder to judge whether each token is plausible in its context. The two are the same kind of judgment, which explains why the CoLA score reflects the form of the pre-training objective rather than the general quality of the encoder. For this reason, we exclude CoLA when comparing MLM and RTD in Section 3.2.

C.2 Comparison with RTD-Trained Encoders

Following Marone et al. (2025), we do not include RTD-trained encoders such as DeBERTaV3 (He et al., 2023) in Table 3. Prior work has consistently found that they fall far behind on retrieval despite their strength on classification (Warner et al., 2025; Breton et al., 2025; Antoun et al., 2025; Boizard et al., 2025; Marone et al., 2025).

For brevity, we report only the classification and retrieval averages of DeBERTaV3 here, computed as in Figure 1. DeBERTaV3-base achieves 74.2 on classification and 20.7 on retrieval, whereas UltraBERT-150M achieves 75.4 and 45.3, respectively. DeBERTaV3-large achieves 78.1 and 25.8, whereas UltraBERT-380M achieves 78.5 and 48.7. Consistent with prior work, we observe substantially lower retrieval performance, with gaps of 24.6 and 22.9 points at the two sizes.

Appendix D Why KoLeo Increases Effective Rank

In this section, we show that the KoLeo regularizer used in Section 3.3 increases the effective rank of representations. The argument proceeds in three steps: KoLeo maximizes the entropy of the representation distribution, near-maximal entropy forces the second moment to be near-isotropic, and near-isotropy flattens the singular value spectrum, which maximizes the effective rank.

Setup

Let Z∈ℝn×dZ\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} stack the ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized representations z1,…,zn∈𝕊d−1z_{1},\dots,z_{n}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1} of a batch, drawn from the representation distribution PP, and let Σ=𝔼P​[z​z⊤]\Sigma=\mathbb{E}_{P}[zz^{\top}] with eigenvalues λ\lambda. Since ∥z∥=1\lVert z\rVert=1, tr⁡Σ=1\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=1, so λ\lambda lies on the probability simplex. Let UU be the uniform distribution on 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, whose second moment is 1d​Id\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d} by symmetry.

Fact 1 (KoLeo estimates entropy).

Up to a positive scaling and an additive constant, ℒKoLeo\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KoLeo}} is the negative Kozachenko–Leonenko estimate of the entropy of PP (Beirlant et al., 1997; Sablayrolles et al., 2019). Minimizing it therefore maximizes the (estimated) entropy of PP, that is, it minimizes KL(P∥U)\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,U), its divergence from the entropy-maximizing uniform distribution.

Proposition 1 (Near-maximal entropy forces near-isotropy).
∥Σ−1dId∥2≤KL(P∥U)/2.\bigl\lVert\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\bigr\rVert_{2}\;\leq\;\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,U)/2}.
Proof.

Fix a unit vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and consider the test function gv​(z)=(v⊤​z)2g_{v}(z)=(v^{\top}z)^{2}. By Cauchy–Schwarz, 0≤(v⊤​z)2≤∥v∥2​∥z∥2=10\leq(v^{\top}z)^{2}\leq\lVert v\rVert^{2}\lVert z\rVert^{2}=1 for z∈𝕊d−1z\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, so gvg_{v} takes values in [0,1][0,1]. Its means under the two distributions are

𝔼P​[gv]=𝔼P​[v⊤​z​z⊤​v]=v⊤​Σ​v,𝔼U​[gv]=v⊤​(1d​Id)​v=1d,\mathbb{E}_{P}[g_{v}]=\mathbb{E}_{P}\bigl[v^{\top}zz^{\top}v\bigr]=v^{\top}\Sigma v,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{U}[g_{v}]=v^{\top}\bigl(\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\bigr)v=\tfrac{1}{d},

using the second moment of UU from the setup and ∥v∥=1\lVert v\rVert=1. Subtracting the two identities gives

|v⊤​(Σ−1d​Id)​v|=|𝔼P​[gv]−𝔼U​[gv]|.\bigl|v^{\top}\bigl(\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\bigr)v\bigr|=\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{P}[g_{v}]-\mathbb{E}_{U}[g_{v}]\bigr|.

We now bound the right-hand side. Since PP and UU are probability measures, ∫c​d​(P−U)=0\int c\,\mathrm{d}(P-U)=0 for any constant cc, so replacing gvg_{v} by the centered function g~v=gv−12\tilde{g}_{v}=g_{v}-\tfrac{1}{2} leaves the difference of means unchanged while ensuring |g~v|≤12\lvert\tilde{g}_{v}\rvert\leq\tfrac{1}{2}. Hence

|𝔼P​[gv]−𝔼U​[gv]|=|∫g~v​d​(P−U)|≤12​∥P−U∥1=TV⁡(P,U),\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{P}[g_{v}]-\mathbb{E}_{U}[g_{v}]\bigr|=\Bigl|\int\tilde{g}_{v}\,\mathrm{d}(P-U)\Bigr|\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\,\lVert P-U\rVert_{1}=\mathrm{TV}(P,U),

where the last identity is the ℓ1\ell_{1} characterization of the total variation distance. Pinsker’s inequality (Cover and Thomas, 2005) bounds this in turn by the KL divergence, TV⁡(P,U)≤KL(P∥U)/2\mathrm{TV}(P,U)\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,U)/2}. Combining the displays, every unit vector vv satisfies |v⊤​(Σ−1d​Id)​v|≤KL(P∥U)/2\lvert v^{\top}(\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d})v\rvert\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,U)/2}. Since Σ−1d​Id\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d} is symmetric, the spectral theorem gives ∥Σ−1d​Id∥2=sup∥v∥=1|v⊤​(Σ−1d​Id)​v|\lVert\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\rVert_{2}=\sup_{\lVert v\rVert=1}\lvert v^{\top}(\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d})v\rvert, and taking the supremum over vv in the bound above proves the claim. ∎

Proposition 2 (Isotropy deviation equals spectral deviation).
∥Σ−1dId∥2=maxk|λk−1d|.\bigl\lVert\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\bigr\rVert_{2}\;=\;\max_{k}\bigl|\lambda_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}\bigr|.
Proof.

Since Σ\Sigma is symmetric, the spectral theorem provides an orthonormal eigenbasis u1,…,udu_{1},\dots,u_{d} with Σ​uk=λk​uk\Sigma u_{k}=\lambda_{k}u_{k}. Because every vector is an eigenvector of the identity, the subtraction of 1d​Id\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d} preserves this eigenbasis and merely shifts the spectrum,

(Σ−1d​Id)​uk=λk​uk−1d​uk=(λk−1d)​uk,\bigl(\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\bigr)u_{k}=\lambda_{k}u_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}u_{k}=\bigl(\lambda_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}\bigr)u_{k},

so Σ−1d​Id\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d} is diagonalized by the same basis with eigenvalues λk−1d\lambda_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}. Expanding any unit vector as v=∑kck​ukv=\sum_{k}c_{k}u_{k} with ∑kck2=1\sum_{k}c_{k}^{2}=1 then gives

∥(Σ−1dId)v∥2=∥∑kck(λk−1d)uk∥2=∑kck2(λk−1d)2≤maxk(λk−1d)2,\Bigl\lVert\bigl(\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\bigr)v\Bigr\rVert^{2}=\Bigl\lVert\sum_{k}c_{k}\bigl(\lambda_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}\bigr)u_{k}\Bigr\rVert^{2}=\sum_{k}c_{k}^{2}\bigl(\lambda_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}\bigr)^{2}\leq\max_{k}\bigl(\lambda_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}\bigr)^{2},

where the middle identity uses orthonormality and the inequality holds because the sum is a convex combination of the squared shifted eigenvalues. Choosing v=uk∗v=u_{k^{\ast}} for an index k∗k^{\ast} attaining the maximum turns the inequality into an equality. Therefore

∥Σ−1dId∥2=max∥v∥=1∥(Σ−1dId)v∥=maxk|λk−1d|.\bigl\lVert\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\bigr\rVert_{2}=\max_{\lVert v\rVert=1}\Bigl\lVert\bigl(\Sigma-\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}\bigr)v\Bigr\rVert=\max_{k}\bigl|\lambda_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}\bigr|.

∎

Corollary 1 (KoLeo flattens the spectrum).

Combining Fact 1, Propositions 1 and 2,

maxk⁡|λk−1d|≤KL(P∥U)/2.\max_{k}\bigl|\lambda_{k}-\tfrac{1}{d}\bigr|\;\leq\;\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,U)/2}.

Hence, as minimizing ℒKoLeo\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KoLeo}} drives KL(P∥U)\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,U) toward zero, every eigenvalue of Σ\Sigma is confined to a shrinking interval around 1/d1/d and the spectrum flattens.

The batch second moment 1n​Z⊤​Z\tfrac{1}{n}Z^{\top}Z concentrates around Σ\Sigma, and its eigenvalues are the squared singular values of Z/NZ/\sqrt{N}, so the singular values σk\sigma_{k} flatten toward a common value as well. Since the effective rank (Roy and Vetterli, 2007; Garrido et al., 2023) is maximized precisely when the singular values are equal, KoLeo exerts an explicit pressure toward maximal effective rank, consistent with the empirical increases observed when it is added (Zhang et al., 2025a; Letellier et al., 2026).

Appendix E Detailed Evaluation Results

E.1 Reported Baseline Scores

For the baselines in Table 3, we take scores from the literature where available and evaluate the rest with the protocols in Appendix B. GLUE scores are taken from the original papers of RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), MosaicBERT (Portes et al., 2023), NomicBERT (Nussbaum et al., 2025), GTE-en-MLM (Zhang et al., 2024), ModernBERT (Warner et al., 2025), Ettin Encoder (Weller et al., 2026), and NeoBERT (Breton et al., 2025), and the GLUE scores of BERT are taken from Portes et al. (2023). SQuAD 2.0 scores of BERT and RoBERTa-large are taken from Liu et al. (2019). All other scores, including GLUE of LFM2.5-Encoder, SQuAD 2.0 of the remaining models, and the NER, RewardBench, and retrieval benchmarks (BEIR, RAR-b, MLDR, and LongEmbed) of every baseline, are obtained by us. Table 7 verifies that our GLUE protocol reproduces the reported scores of Ettin Encoder within 0.2 points at both sizes.

E.2 Full GLUE Results

Table 8 reports the per-task GLUE scores of Table 3. UltraBERT is the best on most tasks at both sizes, with the exceptions of QQP and CoLA at the base size and QQP, SST-2, MRPC, and CoLA at the medium size, where it stays within 1 point of the best model except for CoLA.

E.3 Full RewardBench Results

Table 9 reports the 4 section scores of RewardBench. UltraBERT is the best on Chat, Chat Hard, and Reasoning at the base size, and on Chat Hard and Safety at the medium size, where Ettin Encoder is slightly ahead on Chat and Reasoning. The largest margin is on Chat Hard, where UltraBERT-380M leads the second best by 4.9 points.

E.4 Full BEIR Results

Table 10 reports the nDCG@10 on each of the 15 BEIR datasets, along with the selected learning rate for MS MARCO fine-tuning. UltraBERT is the best on 10 datasets at the base size and 8 at the medium size, where LFM2.5-Encoder-350M leads on NFCorpus, SciFact, TREC-COVID, and CQADupstack.

E.5 Full LongEmbed Results

Table 11 reports the 6 LongEmbed tasks with the maximum context length of each model. UltraBERT is the best on all tasks at the base size, and at the medium size it leads on all tasks except Needle and 2WikiMultihopQA, where LFM2.5-Encoder-230M is ahead. The largest gains are on the two synthetic tasks, Passkey and Needle, where the 32K context is fully used.

Figure 11 breaks down the Passkey accuracy by document length. Every baseline degrades once the document exceeds its context length: the 512-context models fail beyond 1K tokens, and the 8K-context models, including ModernBERT and Ettin Encoder, drop sharply at 16K and 32K. LFM2.5-Encoder degrades more gracefully but still falls below 90% at 32K. UltraBERT is the only model that retains 99% accuracy at every length up to 32K, at both sizes.
